Reproduce

Each file on this site has commands that rebuild it, verify it and certify it against the oracle. The steps below go from a short self-test to the full divisor search. Each step needs only the files it lists.

Setup

The code is C++20 with no external libraries, and make builds it. The published files were built with GCC 16.1.0 (w64devkit), -std=c++20 -O2 -march=native, on an x86-64 processor with FMA3.

The decoders use integer arithmetic only, so any build can verify and certify a file. The coded trees use floating point when the encoder chooses its models, so another compiler or other flags can change the encoders' output. With that build, the rebuilt files matched their published hashes, and each cell page gives the date.

The commands on this site are the ones the make targets run, with the default folders: data/ for downloads and work/ for intermediate and rebuilt files. N is the number of threads (THREADS, by default every hardware thread). Thread counts change only the time, never the bytes.

1. Self-test

Every tool runs on the 8,241 Carmichael numbers below 1012. Each encoder must reproduce its expected file byte for byte. Each decoder must certify its file against the oracle of that prefix. The divisor search must reproduce its expected output.

make check

2. Verify a file

The file matches its published SHA-256 and decodes without error.

make fetch-111x verify-111x

3. Certify against the oracle

Every decoded Carmichael number equals the oracle's, element by element.

make fetch-oracle certify-111x

4. Rebuild a cell from the oracle

The encoders write the published files byte for byte.

make fetch-oracle rebuild-111

Each cell page lists its inputs and the commands its target runs, starting from the results table. The intermediate files below are shared between cells.

5. Rebuild the d∗ file

The d∗ file stores the chosen divisors. Exporting them and encoding them again gives the published file byte for byte, without the search.

make fetch-111x fetch-oracle rebuild-111x

The target runs:

pwt2_decode data/carmichael-1e24-cell111x-pwt-dstar.pwt2 --emit-paths work/c111x.paths.bin --fields 14
pwt2_encode work/c111x.paths.bin data/carmichael-1e24-oracle.orc1 work/carmichael-1e24-cell111x-pwt-dstar.pwt2 --fields 14 --ctx-set 3 --scratch work/scratch --chunk 33554432 --threads 4

6. Rebuild the oracle from the text

The oracle is built from the published text and decodes back to it byte for byte.

make rebuild-oracle

7. Rerun the divisor search

This is the search that chose d∗. Rebuilding cell 111x does not need it, because the file stores the chosen divisors. The search has not been rerun. It prices candidates in floating point, so a rerun is not known to reproduce the published choice byte for byte.

make search-dstar

The search runs four sweeps, saves its choice as masks, and runs a fifth sweep from them. Then the encoder writes the file:

dsel_set2 --orc1 data/carmichael-1e24-oracle.orc1 --dpaths work/dpaths.bin --sweeps 4 --threads 6 --min-gain 0.01 --check-rebuild --max-overflow 60000000 --chunk 33554432 --scratch work/scratch --masks-out work/dstar_masks4.bin
dsel_set2 --orc1 data/carmichael-1e24-oracle.orc1 --dpaths work/dpaths.bin --sweeps 1 --threads 6 --min-gain 0.01 --check-rebuild --max-overflow 60000000 --chunk 33554432 --scratch work/scratch --masks-in work/dstar_masks4.bin --masks-out work/dstar_masks5.bin --emit work/dstar_paths.bin
pwt2_encode work/dstar_paths.bin data/carmichael-1e24-oracle.orc1 work/carmichael-1e24-cell111x-pwt-dstar.pwt2 --fields 14 --ctx-set 3 --scratch work/scratch --chunk 33554432 --threads 4
